items.text: The Supreme Court ruling denying African American citizenship and limiting congressional power over slavery in the territories, intensifying sectional crisis.
The constitutional changes abolishing slavery and establishing citizenship and voting-rights protections, whose enforcement later weakened substantially.

Make slavery the central causal thread; show how territorial expansion and party collapse made compromise progressively harder; for the war, learn only decisive campaigns; for Reconstruction, focus on citizenship, voting rights and the South’s contested rebuilding.
Do not repeat the FPSC typo “North and East”; the conflict was Union/North versus Confederacy/South.
Do not remove slavery from the centre of the causes; states’-rights arguments were closely tied to preserving slavery.
Do not say Reconstruction permanently secured racial equality; many gains were later rolled back through violence, law and political retreat.
The Missouri Compromise (1820), Compromise of 1850, and Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) attempted to manage sectional conflict over slavery.
Lincoln’s 1860 election was followed by secession; war began at Fort Sumter (April 1861); the Emancipation Proclamation took effect 1 January 1863.
The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments abolished slavery and established citizenship and voting protections, though enforcement later weakened.
Correct the syllabus heading’s error explicitly: Union/North versus Confederacy/South, never “North and East.”
Keep slavery at the analytical centre throughout — every other cause (states’ rights, territorial expansion, party collapse) connects back to it, not around it.
